title: Continental Resources Signs Venezuela Oil Deal as Foreign Investment Returns to Energy Sector

author.name: Business Desk
author.bio: Covering international business, global energy markets, and corporate investments.

seoTitle: Continental Resources Signs Venezuela Oil Deal as Foreign Investment Returns to Energy Sector
seoDescription: Continental Resources signs a deal with PDVSA to develop Venezuela's Ayacucho 2 block as Caracas opens its oil industry to new foreign investment.
seoImageAlt: Continental Resources plans Venezuela oil investment as foreign energy companies return to the Orinoco Belt

content.text: A new wave of foreign investment is beginning to reshape Venezuela's oil industry, with US producer Continental Resources signing a memorandum of understanding with state-run Petróleos de Venezuela, known as PDVSA, to develop the Ayacucho 2 block in the country's vast Orinoco Belt. The agreement, signed on September 16, is one of the latest signs that international energy companies are becoming more willing to commit capital to Venezuela after years of sanctions, underinvestment and declining production. Continental plans to move toward a production-sharing agreement in the coming weeks, while Venezuelan authorities are simultaneously negotiating with other foreign companies across oil and mining.

The Ayacucho 2 project is significant because it sits in the Orinoco Belt, Venezuela's largest oil-producing region and one of the world's most resource-rich petroleum areas. Continental estimates that the block contains about 30 billion barrels of resources in place. Chief Executive Doug Lawler said the company is evaluating possible partners for the greenfield development but intends to retain 100% working interest. Continental has said initial production could begin in as little as 18 months, although the project will first require seismic work, exploration and substantial development activity.

The company is led by founder and Executive Chairman Harold Hamm, a prominent figure in the US oil industry. Hamm has also been a major financial supporter of President Donald Trump and served as an informal energy adviser, giving the Venezuela investment additional significance within Washington's broader effort to encourage US companies to enter the country's energy sector. Reuters reported that Hamm's political relationship with Trump has included more than $2 million in contributions to Trump-aligned campaign committees during the 2024 election cycle. The company's investment decision, however, is being presented primarily as a commercial opportunity based on Venezuela's resource potential and Continental's technical expertise.

The Continental agreement is part of a much wider reopening of Venezuela's energy industry to foreign capital. Venezuelan authorities have been changing the framework for oil projects, with foreign producers increasingly moving toward joint ventures and production-sharing arrangements. The new structure is intended to attract investment while giving international companies greater control over projects and clearer commercial terms. Reuters reported that the reform is part of a broader plan to revive Venezuela's energy sector after years of inadequate investment and sanctions-related constraints.

Chevron is already taking advantage of the changing environment. Earlier in September, the US oil major announced plans to invest more than $7 billion through its Venezuelan joint ventures and increase production to roughly 600,000 barrels per day over five years. The expansion includes additional areas in the Carabobo region of the Orinoco Belt. Chevron said new fiscal, commercial and legal terms would protect its long-term investment, while expected production costs would remain below $20 per barrel.

Chevron's move is particularly important because the company has maintained operations in Venezuela throughout periods when many international competitors left. Chevron has operated in the country since 1923 and currently has three joint ventures. Its existing infrastructure gives it an advantage when expanding production because new developments can use established roads, pipelines, water and power systems rather than requiring an entirely new industrial network. Reuters reported that the company's expanded operations are expected to build on that existing infrastructure.

The prospect of renewed US investment is also drawing companies that previously abandoned Venezuela. ExxonMobil is now negotiating a possible return to the Orinoco Belt, including the Petromonagas project, formerly known as Cerro Negro. Exxon previously held a 41.67% interest in the project before its assets were nationalized by the government of Hugo Chávez in 2007. A return would mark a major reversal for the company, which has remained outside Venezuela for almost two decades.

Exxon's potential re-entry demonstrates both the opportunity and the complexity of Venezuela's oil revival. Petromonagas has one of the country's few functioning upgraders capable of converting the Orinoco's extra-heavy crude into lighter grades suitable for export. But the facility is expected to require maintenance and major repairs after years of inadequate investment. There are also unresolved ownership questions involving Russian interests, illustrating how Venezuela's earlier partnerships with China and Russia could complicate the transition toward a larger US corporate presence.

Not every major US oil company is ready to return. ConocoPhillips, which also left Venezuela after its projects were nationalized in 2007, is holding off on re-entry discussions while seeking payment of roughly $11 billion in awards and other amounts connected to the expropriation of its Venezuelan assets. Reuters reported that international arbitration courts found the expropriations unlawful and awarded billions of dollars to ConocoPhillips, much of which remains unresolved. The company's position illustrates why legal and financial certainty remains a central issue for potential investors.

Venezuela's need for new capital is enormous. The country possesses the world's largest proven crude-oil reserves, but its production has fallen sharply from the more than 3 million barrels per day reached in the late 1990s. Reuters reported that current output is around 1.25 million barrels per day, reflecting years of underinvestment, operational problems and sanctions. Reversing that decline requires more than drilling additional wells. Venezuela needs new equipment, upgraded pipelines, refinery maintenance, modern oilfield services, reliable electricity and large-scale infrastructure investment.

Washington is encouraging that investment as part of a broader effort to rebuild Venezuela's energy industry. The Trump administration has promoted a roughly $100 billion reconstruction plan for the sector and has urged American oil companies to participate. The policy has opened a path for companies such as Continental, while also supporting larger expansions by established operators such as Chevron. Reuters reported that US investment is being encouraged with the aim of increasing Venezuelan output and directing more commodity exports toward American markets.

The investment wave is not restricted to crude oil. Venezuelan authorities also signed a separate agreement on September 16 allowing New York-based Heeney Capital, together with commodities trader Mercuria Energy, to operate and export from the Choco gold mine in southern Venezuela. The partnership is expected to last 30 years, with initial investment estimated at up to $1 billion. The simultaneous agreements for gold and oil suggest that the reopening of Venezuela's resource sector is intended to attract foreign capital across multiple commodities rather than focusing exclusively on petroleum.

Other international companies are also positioning themselves for the reopening. Reuters previously reported that Italy's Eni, Swedish investment firm KEO Capital and energy company Primavera were among firms preparing additional agreements. A Florida-based company, Denarius Holding Group, also announced a 20-year agreement to operate an oil project. These developments point to a broader competitive environment in which Caracas is seeking external financing, technology and operational expertise to restart projects that struggled under state-led management and years of sanctions.

For the global oil market, the potential return of Venezuela as a larger producer is strategically important. Venezuela's reserves are enormous, but increasing production quickly is difficult because much of its crude is heavy or extra-heavy and requires specialized infrastructure and upgrading capacity. Even if new investors move rapidly, meaningful production increases are likely to take time. That means the latest agreements should be viewed as the beginning of a rebuilding process rather than an immediate flood of additional oil onto global markets.

The commercial appeal of the Orinoco Belt nevertheless remains strong. Continental and other producers see the scale of the resource base as an opportunity to establish long-lived projects. Existing infrastructure in some areas can lower development costs, while higher oil prices can improve the economics of technically challenging heavy-crude operations. Chevron has said that its expanded projects should have production costs below $20 per barrel, a level that could provide significant operating flexibility if those estimates are achieved.

At the same time, foreign investors face political, legal and operational risks. Venezuela's history of nationalizations remains an important consideration for companies whose investments are designed to operate over decades. Investors must also assess the durability of new contractual arrangements, the treatment of existing Chinese and Russian stakes, access to infrastructure and the ability to repatriate profits. Exxon’s negotiations demonstrate that ownership structures from earlier partnerships can remain relevant even as new investment rules are introduced.

There is also a significant question over how quickly Venezuela can translate new foreign investment into production growth. Oilfield development requires drilling programmes, seismic surveys, pipelines, processing equipment and skilled workers. Continental's statement that first output from Ayacucho 2 could begin in about 18 months represents an ambitious timeline for a greenfield project that still requires substantial exploration and development work. The ultimate schedule will depend on the final production-sharing agreement and the availability of equipment, financing and supporting infrastructure.

The reopening could have broader consequences for Venezuela's economy as well. Higher oil production would potentially increase government revenues, foreign-exchange earnings and demand for local services. International energy companies could create business opportunities for oilfield-equipment suppliers, engineering firms, logistics operators and construction companies. Reuters has already reported a surge in US shipments of second-hand drilling equipment and oilfield machinery to Venezuela as companies prepare for higher activity.

For US businesses, Venezuela is becoming a new frontier at a time when energy markets are under pressure from geopolitical disruptions elsewhere. The Iran conflict has pushed global oil prices higher and increased concerns about supply security. Additional Venezuelan production cannot solve short-term disruptions in the Middle East, but over time it could add another source of heavy crude to international markets and strengthen US access to supplies from a geographically close producer.

The reopening also changes the competitive balance inside Venezuela's energy sector. US companies are receiving strong encouragement from Washington, while the Trump administration is simultaneously seeking to reduce the influence of China and Russia in strategic Venezuelan industries. Yet Venezuelan officials have said existing agreements involving Chinese and Russian partners remain valid. The result is likely to be a mixed investment landscape rather than an immediate replacement of all previous foreign operators.

For Continental Resources, the Ayacucho 2 agreement represents a significant international expansion opportunity. The company is best known for its US shale operations, particularly in the Bakken and other domestic producing regions. Moving into Venezuela's heavy-oil environment gives Continental the chance to apply its technical and operational capabilities to a very different resource base while gaining exposure to one of the world's largest untapped or underdeveloped oil opportunities.

The investment also comes as the Venezuelan government tries to restore credibility with foreign investors. The new agreements are intended to provide clearer commercial and legal terms than those available during previous periods of state dominance. Whether investors ultimately view those reforms as durable will depend on how the contracts are implemented, whether existing disputes are resolved and whether new projects can operate without unexpected regulatory changes.

The immediate market reaction to Continental's agreement is less important than what it represents: another American energy producer is preparing to put capital and expertise into Venezuela. Chevron is expanding, Exxon is considering a return, Eni and other international companies are negotiating projects, and equipment suppliers are already moving into the country. The pattern suggests that Venezuela's oil sector is shifting from a period of isolation toward a more internationally financed model.

For the global energy industry, the reopening offers a potentially important long-term source of supply. For Venezuela, it provides a possible route toward rebuilding an industry that once generated enormous export revenues but has suffered from years of deterioration. And for US energy companies, it opens a resource base that was largely inaccessible for decades. Continental's Ayacucho 2 agreement may therefore be one of the early building blocks of a much broader transformation in Venezuela's oil industry.
What to Watch Next:

The next key milestone is the production-sharing agreement between Continental Resources and PDVSA, expected within weeks. Markets will also watch Continental's seismic and exploration programme, any final investment decision and the timeline for first production. Beyond Ayacucho 2, attention will remain on Chevron's $7 billion expansion, Exxon's negotiations over Petromonagas and whether other US producers decide to return to Venezuela as new investment rules take effect.
